parts.name: The upper city
parts.stand: Just inside the upper gate, at the edge of the open market square, facing downhill.

paras.t: Welcome to Ephesus. Under the Romans this was the capital of their province of Asia, and the geographer Strabo ranked it second only to Rome itself.
First, the heat. Summer noons here push 36 or 37 degrees Celsius, and there's little shade. Wear a hat, carry water, and watch your feet on the old marble.
The Greek city was built in the 10th century BC, and since 2015 the ruins have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site. We'll walk the way most people do, north and downhill, so the slope works for us.

Around you is the upper city: a market square, the scrappy remains of the Baths of Varius, a colonnaded walkway, and the Odeon, a little roofed theater for plays and concerts, with seats for about 1,500 people. A citizen named Publius Vedius Antoninus and his wife built it around 150 AD.

How many people lived here? Older books said up to 225,000. Scholars today call that unrealistic. Mountains, the coast and the quarries hemmed the city in. Recent estimates differ widely; one puts the population between 33,600 and 56,000.

parts.name: Curetes Street
parts.stand: At the Gate of Hercules, at the top of the marble street that slopes away downhill.

paras.t: This is Curetes Street, the main boulevard of the ancient city, leading downhill toward the library.

UNESCO calls it an old processional way, lined with grand Roman monuments. Along this stretch, watch for a big public fountain, the Fountain of Trajan. A leading citizen, Claudius Aristion, paid for it and the water system from 102 AD, and the inscription makes very sure you know who paid.

parts.name: The Temple of Hadrian
parts.stand: Farther down Curetes Street, in front of the small Temple of Hadrian, with the roofed Terrace Houses across the street behind you.

paras.t: This compact little building is the Temple of Hadrian, from the 2nd century, stood up again from its own surviving pieces. Look for Medusa among the carvings on its porch.

The carved panels up top are casts; the originals are in the Ephesus Archaeological Museum. One shows the city's founder from legend, Androklos, a prince of Athens, with his dog. The story goes that an oracle told him a fish and a boar would show him the way, and he founded Ephesus where that came true.
Was it Hadrian's temple from the start? Nobody's sure. The dedication to the emperor may have come later.

parts.name: The Terrace Houses
parts.stand: Turn around to face the slope with the big protective roof, across the street from the temple.

paras.t: Up on this slope lived the rich. The Terrace Houses are six luxury Roman homes, with mosaics on the floors and paintings on the walls, kept under that big roof.

The oldest goes back to the first century BC, and some were still lived in until the seventh century AD. UNESCO singles out Terrace House 2, with its wall paintings, mosaics and marble paneling, as a picture of how the upper levels of society lived.
If you go inside, take the stairs and walkways slowly, and hold the rails.

And everyone else? Farther along the main street, by a monument called the Octagon, is the public latrine, a marble 48-seater. Only the people in these houses and a handful of other very rich families had their own toilets. The latrine was roofed, and used water from the baths ran beneath the seats.

parts.name: The Library of Celsus
parts.stand: At the foot of Curetes Street, in front of the library steps, facing the two-story façade.

paras.t: And here it is, the Library of Celsus. A Roman consul named Aquila ordered it in the 110s as a monument to his father, Celsus, a former governor of Asia. It was finished after Aquila's own death. Celsus himself lies in a marble sarcophagus in a crypt beneath it.

It was a working library too, believed to have held around 12,000 scrolls, third in the Greek and Roman world after Alexandria and Pergamum. It faces east, so the reading room caught the morning light.

In 262 a fire gutted the inside, books and all. Nobody knows whether an earthquake or a Gothic invasion started it; the city seems to have suffered both that year. The façade stood alone until an earthquake in the 10th or 11th century brought it down, and archaeologists put it back up between 1970 and 1978.

Look at the four niches on the lower level, between the columns. Each holds a woman standing for a virtue: Sophia, wisdom; Episteme, knowledge; Ennoia, intelligence; and Arete, excellence. The statues there now are not the originals. And the whole front uses false perspective, so it looks bigger and grander than it really is.
One small thing most people miss: on the second step from the top of the staircase, someone carved a seven-branched menorah, about 8 inches across. Nobody knows exactly when.

parts.name: The Great Theater
parts.stand: Walk on from the library to the Great Theater, and stand at the bottom, looking up at the seats.

paras.t: This is the Great Theater. Acts, chapter nineteen, tells how the whole city was filled with confusion, and a crowd rushed with one accord into the theatre, having caught two of Paul's companions, Gaius and Aristarchus. Later, all with one voice, about the space of two hours, they cried out, Great is Diana of the Ephesians.
It's set into the hillside, built from 200 BC, enlarged in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD, and never roofed. Figures for its size differ: around 24,000 seats, or 25,000.

How did the riot start? Acts says Paul preached in this city, in the synagogue for three months, then daily in the school of one Tyrannus for two years, so that all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word.

Then a silversmith named Demetrius, who made silver shrines for Diana, the goddess the Greeks called Artemis, gathered the craftsmen. Sirs, he said, ye know that by this craft we have our wealth. This Paul hath persuaded and turned away much people, saying that they be no gods, which are made with hands. Not only this our craft is in danger, but also that the temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised.

And Paul? He wanted to go in to the people, but the disciples suffered him not, and friends among the chief men of Asia begged him not to adventure himself into the theatre. Acts adds a very human detail: the more part knew not wherefore they were come together.

In the end the town clerk calmed them. These men, he said, are neither robbers of churches, nor yet blasphemers of your goddess. We are in danger to be called in question for this day's uproar. And he dismissed the assembly.
If you climb the seats for the view, go slowly. The stone steps are steep and uneven.

parts.name: Harbor Street and farewell
parts.stand: At the top of the broad avenue running west from the theater, looking down it toward the old harbor.

paras.t: This avenue ran down to the harbor, the life of the city. But the river slowly silted it up, and today the old harbor lies about 5 kilometers inland.

Paul left Ephesus after the riot. Later, Acts, chapter twenty, says, he sent from Miletus to Ephesus and called the elders of the church. He told them they would see his face no more, and reminded them of the words of the Lord Jesus: It is more blessed to give than to receive. And they all wept sore, and fell on Paul's neck, and kissed him, and accompanied him unto the ship.

The street is the Arcadiane, named for the emperor Arcadius, who reigned from 395 to 408 and rebuilt it as a grand avenue to impress arrivals. Near the lower gate is the Church of Mary, probably where the Council of Ephesus met in 431. About 250 bishops condemned the teaching of Nestorius and declared Mary Theotokos, the Mother of God.

One more voice. In Revelation, chapter two, Ephesus is the first of the seven churches addressed: I know thy works, and thy labour, and thy patience. Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love.
Take a last look down this street before you go. And carry that letter's question with you: what was your first love, and have you left it?
